blocks.text: A low-rank approximation is useful when a matrix acts strongly along only a few directions. Instead of retaining all singular components, keep the largest r and discard the rest. The reconstructed array has the same shape as the input, but its action is restricted to at most r independent directions. The exercise returns that reconstructed array, not the factor matrices.
Return the best rank-r approximation in Frobenius norm using truncated SVD. Rank may be zero and cannot exceed the smaller matrix dimension.

The singular value decomposition writes a real matrix as UΣVᵀ. Columns of U and V are orthonormal directions, and nonnegative singular values measure the strength of each paired direction. Matrix rank counts independent directions, not the number of stored entries.

For the illustrated symmetric matrix, the singular values are 4 and 2. Keeping only the first creates a rank-one matrix with every entry equal to 2. The residual is [[1,−1],[−1,1]]. Its entries are not individually tiny, yet its squared Frobenius error is exactly the discarded singular value squared, namely 4.

blocks.text: Connect the picture to the mathematics

blocks.caption: r is the retained rank. The Frobenius norm squares every matrix entry, sums those squares, and takes the square root.

blocks.text: Change the retained rank from one to two. The second direction restores the information that rank one removed. This illustrates the optimality guarantee: truncated SVD minimizes Frobenius error among rank-r matrices. It does not guarantee the best task-specific prediction accuracy, because a small singular component might still be important for a downstream decision.

The supplied implementation allows rank zero, producing an all-zero approximation, and rejects a rank larger than the smaller matrix dimension. NumPy returns singular values in descending order. Multiplying the columns of U by their corresponding singular values before multiplying by Vh reconstructs the retained components. Watch broadcasting carefully in that expression: scaling the wrong axis changes the matrix. Repeated singular values can make individual singular vectors nonunique even though the best achievable error is well defined.
